phonemes.desc: Rounded [w] plus long close front [iː], then alveolar affricate [t͡s] — the beginning of huītzilin, the Nahuatl word for 'hummingbird.'
Close front [i], alveolar lateral [l], and short [o]: the -il- tail of huītzilin plus the ligature -o- that joins it to ōpōchtli in the compound.
Voiceless bilabial stop [p] plus long back rounded [oː] plus voiceless postalveolar affricate [t͡ʃ]; ōpōchtli means 'left-handed,' also associated with the south.
Lateral affricate [tɬ] plus close front [i], the absolute suffix closing the noun.

pronunciation.approximation: 'weet-see-loh-POCH-tlee' — the 'tz' is 'ts,' the 'ch' is as in 'church,' and the final -tli is one released sound.

kin.label: Classical Nahuatl
kin.form: Huītzilōpōchtli — 'Left-Handed Hummingbird' or 'Hummingbird of the South'

pronunciation.note: The etymology is debated. The most widely accepted analysis takes huītzilin 'hummingbird' + ōpōchtli 'left/south,' joined by the ligature -o-, with a possible interpretation of the hummingbird as the soul of the warrior returning from death. Tier 1: the three macrons preserve the long vowels of huītzilin and ōpōchtli (per Karttunen), distinctive features the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: The Left-Handed Hummingbird
domains.subtitle: Sun, War, and the Mexica Patron
domains.lead: Huītzilōpōchtli is the southern sun in his hummingbird form, the god who led the Mexica out of Aztlān and guided them to the island where Tenochtitlan would rise. He is the warrior's reward and the warrior's demand: the fallen soldier becomes a hummingbird in his paradise, but the sun itself requires human hearts to rise again. In him, tribal patronage, solar theology, and imperial militarism became inseparable.

cards.name: The Sun at Zenith
cards.desc: He is the sun in its rising and midday strength, the southern brilliance that drives away the stars.

cards.name: War and the Warrior's Death
cards.desc: Dead warriors accompanied the rising sun from the east and were reborn as hummingbirds and butterflies; the cihuateteo, women who died in childbirth, escorted the sun toward the west as feared spirits.

cards.name: Tribal Guide
cards.desc: He appeared to the Mexica leaders in dreams and omens, directing the long migration to the promised land.

cards.name: Sacrificial Sustenance
cards.desc: The sun's daily battle against darkness required nourishers of blood and hearts; Huītzilōpōchtli was the hungry sun itself.

mythology.lead: Huītzilōpōchtli's mythology is inseparable from the origin story of the Mexica people. He is the divine ancestor who led the migration, chose the site of Tenochtitlan, defeated the lunar forces arrayed against his mother, and buried an enemy's heart beneath the founding sign of the city.

myths.title: The Birth at Coatepec
myths.text: Cōātlīcue, 'She of the Serpent Skirt,' conceived while sweeping the temple on Coatepec, 'Serpent Mountain': a ball of hummingbird feathers drifted down and she tucked it into her waistband. Her daughter Coyolxāuhqui, 'She of the Golden Bells', and her four hundred brothers, the Centzōn Huītznāhua, were shamed by the unexplained pregnancy and attacked their own mother, Coyolxāuhqui leading the charge with bells ringing on her cheeks. As they closed in, Huītzilōpōchtli sprang from Cōātlīcue's womb fully armed, his face painted, his left leg slender, the xiuhcoatl fire-serpent blazing in his hand (Florentine Codex III). He struck off his sister's head and shattered her body at the mountain's foot — her head he hurled into the sky as the moon, her brothers scattering as the stars. The myth reads like a charter for Mexica sovereignty: the new sun is born by dismembering the old night, and the temple where it happened was rebuilt at the center of Tenochtitlan.

myths.title: The Heart of Copil
myths.text: The migration legend has a dark twin. Copil, son of the sorceress Malinalxōchitl, had sworn vengeance on the Mexica for the wrongs done to his mother; he shadowed the wandering tribe and reported its movements to its enemies, so that everywhere it settled it was attacked. Huītzilōpōchtli ordered his priests to seize the spy, and Copil was sacrificed and his heart cut out. By the god's own command the heart was buried in the reeds of Lake Texcoco — and from it grew a great nopal cactus where no cactus should be, an eagle perched upon it devouring a serpent. That was the sign the god had promised generations before, marking the island of Tenochtitlan (Florentine Codex III; Crónica Mexicayotl). The myth ties the founding sign to a buried enemy: the city's emblem grows out of a heart once set against it — a compact image of how Mexica order converted opposition into ground. The Templo Mayor was raised beside that marsh exactly, and its stairway staged the Coatepec battle in stone.

myths.title: The Journey from Aztlān
myths.text: The Mexica left their ancestral home of Aztlān, 'the Place of the Herons', under Huītzilōpōchtli's direct guidance. The god spoke through his priests and in omens, instructing the people to call themselves Mēxihcah and to search for a promised sign: an eagle perched on a cactus devouring a snake. The wander lasted generations — through Tollan, through the years of servitude at Azcapotzalco, through every settlement that proved not yet the one — and the god's demands grew fiercer as the journey lengthened, the priests carrying his image and voice ahead of the people (Anales de Cuauhtitlan; Crónica Mexicayotl). At last the sign appeared on a small island in Lake Texcoco, and there Tenochtitlan was founded, traditionally in 1325 CE. The myth's logic is the logic of chosen peoples everywhere: suffering on the road is proof of the destination, and the god who made you wander is the god who tells you when to stop. What distinguishes the Mexica version is its candor about the cost — the wandering god is a war god, and the promised land arrives with its altar already built.

myths.title: The Sun's Daily Battle
myths.text: Huītzilōpōchtli is identified with the sun in its southern strength — his very name points south — the star that rises each morning after a night-long passage through the underworld, where the stars and the dead mass against it. To arm him for that battle the Nahua offered the most precious food they possessed: human hearts, 'the nourishment that makes the sun move' (Florentine Codex VI). The warrior who died in battle or on the sacrificial stone was honored above all others: he accompanied the sun from the east for four years and then returned to earth as a hummingbird or a butterfly, sipping nectar forever; the woman who died in childbirth, the cihuapipiltin, marched the opposite escort westward and became a feared spirit. The theology binds biology, warfare, and astronomy into one economy: every birth, every battle, every dawn is the same transaction paid in blood. To feed the sun is to join it — and the hummingbird, iridescent and tireless, is the soldier's final rank.

lore.syncretism: Huītzilōpōchtli has no close non-Nahua equivalent; he is a specifically Mexica tribal god elevated to solar supremacy. Within Mesoamerica he shares solar-warrior traits with the Maya sun god K'inich Ajaw and with Mixtec and Zapotec martial deities. After the conquest, Spanish writers sometimes identified him with Hercules or with the Christian devil — comparisons shaped more by revulsion at human sacrifice than by theological correspondence. In the colonial period his festivals were suppressed and his temples dismantled, but his birth story survived in the Florentine Codex, copied out by Nahua scribes under Franciscan supervision. Modern nationalist movements have sometimes celebrated Huītzilōpōchtli as a symbol of indigenous resistance, while other interpreters — including Indigenous scholars — emphasize the imperial violence carried out in his name. Both receptions are true to different layers of the source: a tribal patron turned imperial sun.
lore.culturalLegacy: Huītzilōpōchtli remains one of the most recognizable figures of Aztec religion, embodied in the Templo Mayor and the Calendar Stone's central solar imagery. In Mexico today he appears in murals, museum branding, and nationalist iconography, often as a symbol of Mexica identity and pre-Columbian grandeur; Mexico City's coat of arms still shows his founding sign, the eagle on the cactus. Critics and Indigenous scholars caution against romanticizing the militarized theology associated with his cult, even as archaeologists continue to reveal the sophistication of the ritual city built in his honor. The 1978 discovery of the Coyolxāuhqui stone re-centered his birth myth in Mexican public life — and the excavated Templo Mayor, at the heart of the modern capital, keeps the question of what his temple cost permanently on the national agenda.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Huītzilōpōchtli is the sun as hungry deity, the warrior as ancestor, the nation as divine mission. His mythology binds together birth, migration, war, and sacrifice into a single imperial narrative. For the Mexica, to worship him was to be Mēxihcah; to die for him was to become light.

Modern readers often recoil at the human sacrifice central to his cult. But Huītzilōpōchtli also raises a question that every civilization faces: what does the community owe to the forces that sustain it? The Nahua answer was literal and terrible — hearts and blood. Our answers are usually more abstract but no less consequential. To name Huītzilōpōchtli with its long vowels restored is to keep the question alive in its most uncompromising form.

lore.archaeology: Huītzilōpōchtli's principal shrine was the southern half of the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan, excavated extensively from 1978 onward. The Coyolxāuhqui stone disk at the base of the temple stairway depicts his defeated sister and dramatizes the Coatepec myth; the great serpent heads flanking the stairway repeat the sacred mountain's name in stone. The Calendar Stone (Piedra del Sol), although not exclusively solar, is popularly associated with Huītzilōpōchtli's sun cult. Pictorial manuscripts such as the Codex Borbonicus, Codex Telleriano-Remensis, and Codex Azcatitlan preserve his migration myths and calendar festivals. Recent tunnel and offering excavations at the Templo Mayor have recovered caches of sacrificial victims and sacred objects that give his cult a direct, unflinching material record.
